question: IA
answer:
INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (IA) — QUALIFICATIONS AND AUTHORITY RELATING TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS
FAA-AMT context / 14 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 65, Subpart D / source: ecfr.gov

====================================================================
0. ANSWER IN ONE PARAGRAPH
====================================================================
The qualification requirements are in 14 CFR 65.91(c). Five criteria must all be met: (1) hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective and in effect for a total of at least 3 years; (2) have been actively engaged for at least the 2-year period before applying in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR; (3) have a fixed base of operations at which the holder may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week (it need not be where the authority is exercised); (4) have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and (5) pass a written test on ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after MAJOR REPAIRS AND MAJOR ALTERATIONS and annual and progressive inspections performed under Part 43. The authority that qualification confers over major alterations is in 65.95(a)(1): the IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (EXCEPT any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with Part 43, IF the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator. Both conditions are conjunctive: no Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft, and no approval of work not done to Administrator-approved technical data.

====================================================================
1. SCOPE NOTE — TWO READINGS, BOTH ANSWERED
====================================================================
The question 'qualifications for inspection authorization regarding major alterations' has two distinct readings, and the regulation answers them in two different sections. Both are given, because a mechanic pursuing the IA needs both and conflating them is the classic error:
  READING A — Who is eligible to HOLD an IA (the entry qualification). Governed by 14 CFR 65.91. The link to major alterations is 65.91(c)(5): the written test is expressly a test on returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations.
  READING B — What an IA may DO about a major alteration once qualified (the privilege and its limits). Governed by 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1), with accomplishment and recording cross-referenced to Part 43.
A statement of eligibility (Reading A) is NOT a statement of authority (Reading B). Meeting 65.91(c) does not enlarge the 65.95(a)(1) privilege.

All five are conjunctive — 'an applicant must' do all of (1) through (5). Failure of any one disqualifies.

Note on 65.91(c)(5): this is the direct statutory hook between the QUALIFICATION and MAJOR ALTERATIONS. The IA written test is not a general airworthiness test; its stated scope is post-maintenance return to service after major repair and major alteration, plus annual and progressive inspection under Part 43.

====================================================================
4. THE MAJOR-ALTERATION PRIVILEGE — 65.95(a)(1) DECOMPOSED INTO FIVE CONDITIONS
====================================================================
An approval action is within the IA privilege ONLY if all five conditions below hold. Read them as an AND-gate; any single failure takes the action outside 65.95(a)(1).

 C1. Actor: the person holds an inspection authorization. (Per 65.91(c)(1) the underlying mechanic certificate must remain currently effective for the authorization to be exercisable — see the CITE-CHECK item on 65.93 in section 6.)
 C2. Subject: an aircraft or related part or appliance. The provision reaches parts and appliances, not only complete aircraft.
 C3. Exclusion: NOT an aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121. This exclusion is written into the privilege itself and is not waivable by the IA.
 C4. Event: a MAJOR repair or MAJOR alteration has been accomplished, and the action is inspection and approval for return to service after it. (See CITE-CHECK item on the Part 1 definition of 'major alteration' in section 6 — the major/minor line determines whether this provision is the operative one at all.)
 C5. Technical basis: the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator, and the approval for return to service is made in accordance with Part 43. Work accomplished on other than Administrator-approved technical data is outside this privilege.

Operational consequence of C5 (the most frequently failed condition): the IA's signature under 65.95(a)(1) is an approval of work already accomplished to approved data. It is not authority to create, substitute, or waive the technical data. FAA guidance reinforces that major repairs and alterations must be accomplished using FAA-approved technical data.

====================================================================
5. WHAT THIS DOES NOT AUTHORIZE (limits stated in, or implied by, the verified text)
====================================================================
 L1. No approval for return to service of a major repair or major alteration on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program — express carve-out in 65.95(a)(1).
 L2. No approval where the work was not done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator — express condition in 65.95(a)(1).
 L3. No inference of broader authority. Any claim that an IA may approve major alterations outside the conditions of 65.95(a)(1) — for example, without approved technical data, or on Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft — is UNVERIFIED and should be treated as incorrect until a citation is produced.
 L4. Eligibility does not equal authority. Satisfying 65.91(c) confers no privilege by itself; the privileges are those stated in 65.95.

====================================================================

7. HOW TO STATE THIS TO A MECHANIC IN ONE SCREEN
====================================================================
To be eligible for an IA you need: an A&P mechanic certificate, currently effective, with both ratings in effect a total of at least 3 years; at least 2 years immediately before application actively engaged in maintaining 14 CFR-certificated/maintained aircraft; a fixed base of operations where you can be reached during a normal working week; the equipment, facilities, and inspection data to do the inspections; and a passing score on the written test — which is specifically a test on returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and on annual and progressive inspections under Part 43. Once you hold it, 65.95(a)(1) lets you inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft, part, or appliance after a major repair or major alteration — but not on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program, and only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator. Both limits are in the regulation text itself.

# Inspection Authorization (IA) — Qualification Requirements Bearing on Major Alterations

Source of authority: eCFR, Title 14 (current). Quoted text below is verbatim from eCFR pages fetched 2026-11-15 (hashes in §8). Anything not quoted is labelled [verify] and must be read verbatim on eCFR before being relied on in a compliance finding.

## 1. Bottom line

There is no separate IA qualification for major alterations. The qualification standard is the single eligibility rule at **14 CFR § 65.91(c)**. Its relevance to major alterations comes from the privilege at **14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1)**, which is what an IA holder (and only an IA holder, among mechanics) may exercise after a major repair or major alteration. In other words: qualify for the IA under § 65.91(c), and the major-alteration return-to-service privilege under § 65.95(a)(1) comes with it — subject to the conditions embedded in that paragraph.

Authority chain: Part 65, Subpart E (§§ 65.91–65.95) + Part 43 (§§ 43.3, 43.7, Appendix A) + § 1.1 (definitions). Advisory material (FAA Order 8900.1, ACs, the FAA-AMT handbooks) explains but does not create the qualification.

## 2. Regulatory map

| Question | Governing text |
|---|---|
| Who is eligible to hold an IA | 14 CFR § 65.91(c) — five criteria |
| How long the IA lasts | 14 CFR § 65.92 [verify] |
| How it is renewed | 14 CFR § 65.93 [verify] |
| What the IA may approve, incl. after a major alteration | 14 CFR § 65.95(a)(1) |
| What else the IA may do (annual / progressive inspections) | 14 CFR § 65.95(a)(2) [verify] |
| Limits on the privilege | 14 CFR § 65.95(b) [verify] |
| Who may approve for return to service at all | 14 CFR § 43.7(a), (b) [verify] |
| What counts as a major alteration | 14 CFR § 1.1; Part 43 Appendix A |
| That Appendix A is the operative list | 14 CFR § 43.3 |

## 3. The qualification itself — § 65.91(c)

Verbatim (eCFR, § 65.91(c)):

> “(c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.”

Structured for a compliance file:

| # | Criterion | Threshold | Evidence an auditor would expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| (c)(1) | Mechanic certificate with **both** Airframe and Powerplant ratings, each currently effective | Each rating in effect for a total of **at least 3 years** | Certificate with A and P ratings, issue dates |
| (c)(2) | Actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | **At least the 2-year period** immediately before application | Employment/activity records, logbook or employer attestation |
| (c)(3) | Fixed base of operations, reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | No numeric threshold | Address/phone on application; note the base need not be where authority is exercised |
| (c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | No numeric threshold | Inventory/list of inspection data (specs, ADs, service data) and tooling |
| (c)(5) | Pass the written test on inspecting to safety standards for return to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual/progressive inspections under Part 43 | Pass | Test results / FAA notification |

Note on (c)(5): the written test is itself the point at which the rule ties IA qualification directly to major alterations — the test content is expressly about returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations. That is the only place in § 65.91 where major alterations appear.

## 4. The major-alteration privilege the qualification unlocks — § 65.95(a)(1)

Verbatim (eCFR, § 65.95(a)(1)):

> “(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and”

Three conditions are embedded in that single sentence, and all three must be satisfied before the IA may sign:

1. **Scope exclusion** — not applicable to aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.
2. **Part 43 compliance** — the work must have been done in accordance with Part 43.
3. **Approved data** — the work must have been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator.

What the privilege is **not**: it is a *return-to-service approval* privilege. It is not authority to approve the alteration data itself. Data approval is a separate act (STC under Part 21, or a field approval processed through FAA Order 8900.1) [verify Part 21 citation for the specific alteration route]. § 65.95(a)(1) presupposes that the data is already “approved by the Administrator.”

## 5. What “major alteration” means, and who may otherwise approve

- § 43.3, verbatim: “Those items, the performance of which is a major alteration, a major repair, or preventive maintenance, are listed in appendix A.” Part 43 Appendix A is therefore the operative list of what is a major alteration (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance categories).
- § 1.1 supplies the general definition of major alteration (an alteration not listed in the aircraft/engine/propeller specifications that might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other airworthiness qualities, or that is not done per accepted practices / cannot be done by elementary operations) [verify exact § 1.1 wording on eCFR].
- § 43.7(b) is the general gate: a mechanic certificate holder or an IA may approve for return to service as provided in Part 65 [verify exact wording]. The practical effect is that for major repairs/alterations the Part 65 gate resolves to the IA under § 65.95(a)(1).

## 6. Compliance checklist / common failure points

- **Both ratings, not just the certificate.** § 65.91(c)(1) requires an airframe rating *and* a powerplant rating, each effective for a total of at least 3 years. A mechanic certificate with only one rating fails, regardless of total years of experience.
- **Two-year active-engagement window is measured backward from the application date**, and it must be maintenance of aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR — non-certificated or foreign-registry work may not count [verify applicability].
- **Fixed base and inspection data are substantive criteria**, not clerical. § 65.91(c)(3)–(4) can be failed by an applicant with no reachable base or no current inspection data.
- **Do not conflate approval of the alteration with approval for return to service.** The IA signs the return to service; the data must already be Administrator-approved.
- **Do not conflate with other approval holders:** Part 145 repair station approvals, DER/DAR designee approvals, and Part 121 continuous-airworthiness programs each have their own rules; § 65.95(a)(1) expressly excludes Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft.
- **Currency matters.** An IA that has lapsed is not a qualifying IA. See § 7.

## 7. Duration and renewal (adjacent, needed for a live compliance determination)

- § 65.92: an inspection authorization is of limited duration and expires on a fixed calendar date (commonly cited as March 31 of each odd-numbered year) [verify verbatim].
- § 65.93: renewal is activity-based or training-based over the preceding 12 months — typically annual inspections, major repairs/alterations, or progressive inspections at a stated cadence (commonly cited as “for each 90 days”), or completion of an IA refresher course acceptable to the Administrator [verify verbatim; do not rely on the 90-day cadence without reading § 65.93(a)].
- Because the renewal options include major repairs/alterations, an IA whose major-alteration volume is low may need the refresher-course route; that is a planning point, not a qualification point.

## 8. Sources (fetched, with hashes)

| § 65.91 | http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/section-65.91 | 2026-11-15T03:42:17Z | 8dd2b52b76db |
| § 65.95 | http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/section-65.95 | 2026-11-15T03:42:18Z | 04eedc455339 |
| § 43.3 | http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-43/section-43.3 | 2026-11-15T03:42:17Z | b10f62b56b41 |
| Part 65 (XML) | https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/xml/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-part65.xml | — | — |

## 9. Items that must be re-read verbatim on eCFR before being cited in a finding

§ 65.92 (duration and expiration date); § 65.93 (renewal options and cadence); § 65.95(a)(2) and § 65.95(b) (remaining privileges and limitations); § 43.7(a) and (b) (who may approve for return to service); § 1.1 (major alteration definition); Part 43 Appendix A (itemized major alterations); Part 21 (route for approving alteration data). These are identified in the deliverable as background and are marked [verify] wherever stated, so nothing above asserts fetched text that was not fetched.

## 10. Scope note on “FAA-AMT”

The FAA Aviation Maintenance Technician handbooks and the IA-related FAA guidance (FAA Order 8900.1, advisory circulars) are explanatory. They restate § 65.91(c) and § 65.95(a)(1); they do not add qualification criteria and are not the authority to cite. Cite the CFR sections above; cite guidance only as explanatory support.

answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) and Major Alterations — 14 CFR Part 65

**Source basis:** 14 CFR as published on eCFR (ecfr.gov). Primary provisions: part 65 (§§ 65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95) and part 43 (§§ 43.5, 43.7, 43.9; appendix A). FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide* used only for clarifying the IA's major-alteration duty. Paragraph-level verification items are listed in §8 — read §8 before quoting this in a training or enforcement-sensitive document.

---

## 1. Bottom line

There is **no separate 'major alteration' qualification**. The qualification is **holding a valid inspection authorization issued under 14 CFR part 65**, and approving major repairs/major alterations for return to service is the core privilege that authorization exists to confer.

To be **eligible** for an IA under § 65.91(c), an applicant must:

1. Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective and **in effect for a total of at least 3 years**;
2. Have been **actively engaged for at least the 2-year period** before applying in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR chapter I;
3. Have a **fixed base of operations** where reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week;
4. Have available the **equipment, facilities, and inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, and related parts/appliances; and
5. **Pass the IA written test**, which by rule is a test of ability to inspect to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations**, and for annual and progressive inspections under part 43.

Once held, the **major-alteration authority** is § 65.95(a)(1): the IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance **after a major repair or major alteration** accomplished in accordance with part 43, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** — **except** aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness maintenance program under part 121.

---

## 2. Eligibility criteria — § 65.91(c)

| # | Criterion (§ 65.91(c)) | What it means in practice | Evidence an AMT should be able to produce |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mechanic certificate with **airframe and powerplant** ratings, both currently effective, **in effect ≥ 3 years total** | An A-only or P-only certificate does not qualify. The 3 years runs on the ratings, not on time since last employment. | Mechanic certificate; airman registry record showing rating issue dates |
| 2 | **Actively engaged ≥ 2 years** before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter | Must be aircraft work under part 43/part 91/121/135/145 rules, not unrelated mechanical work. | Employment/1099 history, work orders, employer letters, training records |
| 3 | **Fixed base of operations** | A physical location where you can be reached in person or by phone during a normal working week. It need not be where you exercise the authorization. | Address on application; hangar/shop lease or employer statement |
| 4 | **Equipment, facilities, and inspection data** available | Access to current manufacturer maintenance manuals, ADs, type certificate data sheets, approved data, and the tooling/inspection equipment needed. | Subscription/token access to maintenance library; tool inventory; calibrated equipment records |
| 5 | **Pass the written test** under § 65.91(c)(5) | The test is explicitly about returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and about annual/progressive inspections under part 43 — i.e., the major-alteration competency is a *tested* eligibility element, not an add-on. | Passed test report |

Supporting procedural points: application is made **on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator** (§ 65.91(a)); an applicant who meets the section is **entitled** to the authorization (§ 65.91(b)).

---

## 3. What the IA may do with a major alteration — § 65.95(a)(1)

The privilege has four built-in conditions. All four must be satisfied:

1. **The item is an aircraft, or a related part or appliance** — the authority is item-scoped, not a general repair-station approval.
2. **The work was a major repair or major alteration accomplished in accordance with part 43** — the alteration must have been performed under part 43 rules (§ 43.3 persons authorized, § 43.13 performance standards).
3. **The work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** — the IA approves the *work*, not the *data*. Approved data means FAA-approved data (e.g., type certificate data, STC, AD-mandated data, FAA field-approved data, DER-approved data). The IA cannot bootstrap unapproved data into approval by signing for return to service.
4. **The aircraft is not maintained under a part 121 continuous airworthiness maintenance program** — for part 121 CAMP aircraft, that approval is made within the certificate holder's program, not by an IA under § 65.95(a)(1).

Additional duty attached to the major-alteration inspection (FAA *IA Information Guide*): during inspection of major repairs or major alterations, the IA **must also determine that they are compatible with previous repairs and alterations** made to the aircraft. This is a substantive airworthiness finding, not a paperwork step.

Also within the IA's privileges (§ 65.95(a)(2)): perform an annual inspection, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection, per §§ 43.13 and 43.15.

---

## 4. What the IA does not give you (common misreads)

- **It is not a data-approval authority.** No IA signature converts unapproved alteration data into approved data. If no approved data exists, the route is an FAA field approval / DER / STC — not an IA sign-off.
- **It does not cover part 121 CAMP aircraft** under § 65.95(a)(1).
- **It does not expand your rating limits.** The IA sits on top of an A&P certificate; work outside your ratings remains outside them.
- **It is not required for minor alterations/repairs.** Minor work is approved for return to service by a mechanic within the limits of part 65 (see §§ 65.81, 65.85, 65.87); the IA is the part-65 mechanism aimed at major repairs/alterations and annual/progressive inspections.
- **It is not a substitute for the maintenance record entry.** The § 43.5 conditions must still be met (record entry made, repair/alteration form executed, operating limitations/flight manual data revised if changed).

> **Cross-check to read before relying on a single sign-off path:** §§ 65.85(b) and 65.87(b) (airframe and powerplant ratings; additional privileges) bear directly on whether an A&P holding the applicable rating may approve for return to service after a major repair/alteration performed in accordance with approved technical data. Read §§ 65.85 and 65.87 together with § 65.95(a)(1) and § 43.7(b) before deciding who signs a given major alteration. I am flagging this as a required read rather than characterizing its exact scope here (see §8).

---

## 5. Keeping the qualification — duration, currency, renewal (§§ 65.92–65.93)

- **Expiration:** each inspection authorization **expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year** — a 2-year (24-month) cycle.
- **Currency to exercise privileges:** the holder may exercise IA privileges **only while holding a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe rating and a currently effective powerplant rating**.
- **Ceases to be effective** when: the authorization is surrendered, suspended, or revoked; the holder no longer has a fixed base of operations; or the holder no longer has the equipment, facilities, and inspection data required by § 65.91(c)(3)–(4).
- **Return of certificate** on suspension or revocation, as required by the rule.
- **Renewal (§ 65.93):** renewal requires evidence satisfactory to the Administrator of continued qualifying inspection activity and/or completion of refresher training during the 24 months preceding expiration. **The specific activity counts and training-hour thresholds are not reproduced here** — they must be read from the current § 65.93 text before being used as a compliance standard (see §8, item 3).

---

## 6. Documentation chain for a major alteration

| Step | Requirement | Cite |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Work performed by authorized persons to part 43 performance standards | §§ 43.3, 43.13 |
| 2 | Work performed to **approved** technical data | § 65.95(a)(1) (condition on the IA's approval) |
| 3 | Maintenance record entry made | § 43.9; required as a precondition by § 43.5 |
| 4 | FAA Form 337 executed for the major repair/alteration | § 43.9(d); Form 337 instructions |
| 5 | Operating limitations / flight manual data revised if the alteration changes them | § 43.5; § 91.9 |
| 6 | IA inspects, checks compatibility with prior repairs/alterations, and approves for return to service | § 65.95(a)(1); § 43.7(b); FAA *IA Information Guide* |
| 7 | Records retained by the owner/operator | § 91.417 (part 91); corresponding part 121/135 record rules for those operators |

§ 43.7(b) is the bridge provision: *"The holder of a mechanic certificate or an inspection authorization may approve an aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service as provided in Part 65 of this chapter."* Part 65 is therefore where the scope of the IA's approval authority is actually defined.

---

## 7. Applying it — procedure for the AMT

1. **Classify the change.** Determine whether the change is a major alteration under part 43, appendix A (airframe / powerplant / propeller / appliance categories). If minor, the IA path under § 65.95(a)(1) is not the applicable one.
2. **Identify the operator's maintenance program.** If the aircraft is maintained under a part 121 CAMP, stop — § 65.95(a)(1) does not apply; approval is made within that program.
3. **Confirm approved data exists** for the alteration (TC data, STC, AD, field approval, DER data). If only unapproved data exists, obtain approval of the data first; do not proceed to a return-to-service approval.
4. **Verify your own currency before signing anything:** mechanic certificate with both ratings currently effective; IA not expired (expires March 31 of odd-numbered years); fixed base maintained; equipment/facilities/inspection data available (§§ 65.91(c)(3)–(4), 65.92).
5. **Inspect the installed alteration against the approved data** — conformity, workmanship, and effect on the rest of the aircraft.
6. **Assess compatibility** with previous repairs and alterations on the aircraft (FAA *IA Information Guide* duty).
7. **Complete the record:** maintenance record entry (§ 43.9), FAA Form 337 executed (§ 43.9(d)), operating limitations/flight manual data revised if changed (§ 43.5; § 91.9).
8. **Approve for return to service** under § 65.95(a)(1)/§ 43.7(b) and dispose of the Form 337 copies per the form's instructions.

---

## 8. Source verification items (confirm on eCFR before publishing or training from this)

1. **§ 65.91(c)(1)–(5) paragraph text** — the five eligibility criteria above are stated from the rule as commonly reproduced; confirm exact wording and current amendment level at `ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65`.
2. **§ 65.95(a)(1) exact text**, including the part 121 CAMP exclusion wording and the "technical data approved by the Administrator" condition.
3. **§ 65.93 renewal thresholds** — activity counts and refresher-training hours were intentionally omitted here; read them from the current text.
4. **§ 65.92 vs § 65.93 split** (duration vs renewal) and the **subpart designation** for §§ 65.91–65.95 within part 65 — confirm the section-to-subject mapping and URL before citing.
5. **§§ 65.85(b) / 65.87(b)** — read in full to fix the boundary between mechanic and IA approval authority for major repairs/alterations performed to approved data.
6. **§ 43.9(d) and Form 337 execution/disposition requirements** — confirm who executes the form and where copies go.
7. **Currency of the text** — record the eCFR "current as of" date and the amendment number in any downstream document.

**Limits of this answer:** produced without live eCFR access; no amendment level is certified here. Items 1–6 are the only places where paragraph-level precision matters, and each is named so a reviewer can close it in minutes against the current text. Nothing in this answer should be read as FAA legal interpretation.

question: IA
answer:
QUALIFICATIONS FOR INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (IA) WITH RESPECT TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS — 14 CFR (eCFR) ANSWER

====================================================================
0. BOTTOM LINE
====================================================================
Two sections carry the answer, and they answer two different questions that the request conflates:

  * 14 CFR 65.91(c) — the QUALIFICATIONS A PERSON MUST HAVE TO HOLD an inspection authorization at all.
  * 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1) — the CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH the holder may actually inspect and approve for return to service an aircraft or part after a MAJOR ALTERATION.

An IA is not qualified to approve a major alteration merely by holding the authorization. 65.95(a)(1) adds three independent conditions, the controlling one being that the work must have been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator. If the alteration was done to unapproved data, no amount of IA qualification makes the approval valid.

====================================================================
1. SCOPE — HOW I READ THE QUESTION (state these back if wrong)
====================================================================
The request does not say which of three things is wanted. All three are answered below:
  (A) Qualification to HOLD an IA ...................... Section 2
  (B) Qualification/conditions to EXERCISE IA authority on a major alteration ... Section 3
  (C) What counts as a 'major alteration' (the determination the IA must make) ... Section 4
Assumptions used: 14 CFR (eCFR) is the controlling source; the requester is an AMT/student, not an air carrier; Part 91 general aviation context; 'major alteration' in its regulatory sense, not colloquial. Air carrier (Part 121 continuous airworthiness) aircraft are expressly carved out of 65.95(a)(1) and are not covered by this answer.

====================================================================
2. (A) QUALIFICATIONS TO HOLD AN IA — 14 CFR 65.91(c)
====================================================================
The applicant must satisfy ALL of the following (enumerated from 14 CFR 65.91(c); PARAPHRASE — confirm exact wording on the eCFR section page for 65.91 before quoting in any training or enforcement document):

  65.91(c)(1)  Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which has been effective for at least 3 YEARS.
               -> An A-only or P-only certificate does not qualify. Ratings must be current, not suspended/revoked.
  65.91(c)(2)  Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-YEAR period before applying, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter.
               -> Bench/parts/sales/non-aviation time does not count; the activity must be aircraft maintenance under 14 CFR.
  65.91(c)(3)  Have a fixed base of operations.
  65.91(c)(4)  Have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
               -> This is the qualification element most directly tied to major alterations: without access to current approved technical data and the tooling/access to verify conformity, the applicant does not meet (c)(4).
  65.91(c)(5)  Pass a written test on the applicant's ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after MAJOR REPAIRS and MAJOR ALTERATIONS and after annual and progressive inspections.
               -> The IA test itself is a major-alteration test; major alteration approval is a core, tested IA competency, not an incidental privilege.

Application mechanics: the application is made on the form and in the manner prescribed by the Administrator and submitted to the FAA Flight Standards District Office having jurisdiction over the applicant's fixed base of operations (14 CFR 65.91(a)-(b) — PARAPHRASE, verify exact text).

Currency (keeps the qualification alive — 'qualified' requires 'current'):
  * 14 CFR 65.92 — duration: the authorization is effective until March 31 of the first odd-numbered year after issuance unless suspended or revoked. (VERIFY at eCFR 65.92; do not restate as a fixed 24-month term.)
  * 14 CFR 65.93 — renewal: must be renewed before expiration through one of the routes the section lists, which include an FAA-accepted refresher/update training route and activity-based routes. (The specific hour requirement has changed over time; DO NOT state an hour count from this document — read 65.93 as currently published.)
  * Practical effect: a lapsed IA has no 65.95(a)(1) privilege at all, so any major-alteration approval signed by a lapsed holder is not a valid return-to-service approval.

====================================================================
3. (B) QUALIFICATIONS/CONDITIONS TO EXERCISE IA AUTHORITY ON A MAJOR ALTERATION — 14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)
====================================================================
VERBATIM (fetched from eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 65, Subpart D, 65.95):

  '(a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
   (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and'

Decomposed into the conditions the IA must be able to satisfy and document:

  COND-1  The aircraft is NOT maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. (Part 121 aircraft: not an IA function.)
  COND-2  The work was done in accordance with TECHNICAL DATA APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATOR. The IA's qualification here is the demonstrated ability to determine whether the data is FAA-approved and appropriate — i.e., to identify its approval basis (e.g., TC/STC holder data, FAA field approval, design approval via DER/ODA under an approved design approval procedure). The IA does not create or 'bless' data; an IA signature cannot convert unapproved data into approved data. Unapproved-data alterations must be routed to an approval path before an IA can approve for return to service.
  COND-3  The inspection and approval is performed 'in accordance with part 43' — i.e., conformity to the approved data plus the Part 43 performance rules (14 CFR 43.13), and proper record/approval entries.

Supporting Part 43 obligations the IA must be qualified to execute (these are where major-alteration approvals actually fail):
  * 43.5 — no person may approve for return to service an aircraft/part that has undergone maintenance, alteration, etc. unless the required record entry has been made, the repair/alteration form furnished by the Administrator (FAA Form 337) has been executed as prescribed, and weight-and-balance / flight-characteristic changes have been accounted for. (PARAPHRASE — verify exact text.)
  * 43.7 — persons authorized to approve for return to service (this is the authority 65.95(a)(1) plugs the IA into).
  * 43.9 — content/form/disposition of maintenance and alteration records; the major alteration must be recorded, and the Form 337 is the vehicle for major repairs and major alterations.
  * 43.11 — record/approval entries for inspections (annual/progressive) — relevant because a major alteration is frequently encountered during an annual inspection.
  * 43.13 — performance rules: work must be done using methods, techniques, and practices acceptable to the Administrator.
  * 91.417 — operator maintenance record retention (Part 91), so the alteration and 337 are traceable.

Competency statement for the IA role: the IA must be able to (i) classify the change as major or minor, (ii) determine the approval status and applicability of the technical data, (iii) physically inspect for conformity to that data and to 43.13, (iv) confirm weight/balance and operating-limitation impacts are handled, and (v) make the correct record and Form 337 entries and approve for return to service — or refuse approval and return the package to the installer.

====================================================================
4. (C) WHAT 'MAJOR ALTERATION' MEANS — THE THRESHOLD THE IA MUST APPLY
====================================================================
  * 14 CFR 1.1 definition (PARAPHRASE): a major alteration is an alteration not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications that (1) might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness, or (2) is not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations.
  * 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A lists major alterations by category (airframe, powerplant, propeller, appliance) and is the operative checklist.
  * Anything not major is a minor alteration, handled by a certificated mechanic's record entry (43.9) without the 65.95(a)(1) approval path.
  * The major/minor call is a judgment the IA is expected to make and defend; misclassifying a major alteration as minor is the classic violation in this area.

====================================================================
5. BOUNDARIES — WHAT AN IA CANNOT DO (state these alongside the privileges)
====================================================================
  1. Cannot approve a major alteration on an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program (express carve-out in 65.95(a)(1)).
  2. Cannot approve for return to service work performed to data that is not FAA-approved (65.95(a)(1) condition).
  3. Cannot substitute an IA signature for a design approval. DER/ODA approvals are approvals of DATA within an approved design approval procedure; the return-to-service approval after the alteration is by a person authorized under 43.7 / 65.95(a)(1). I am deliberately NOT stating a DER as the return-to-service approver — the cited sources do not support that and it would be a wrong answer.
  4. Cannot exercise any 65.95 privilege while the authorization is expired, suspended, or revoked (65.92/65.93 currency).
  5. NOT A REGULATION, GUIDANCE/PRACTICE ONLY: the expectation that an IA not approve for return to service work the IA personally performed (independence of the inspection function). Verify against current FAA guidance before relying on it as a rule; do not cite it as 14 CFR.

====================================================================
6. PRACTICAL CHECKLIST FOR AN AMT/IA ON A MAJOR-ALTERATION PACKAGE
====================================================================
  [ ] 1. Classify: major vs. minor (Part 43 App. A + 1.1 definition). If minor, 43.9 entry only.
  [ ] 2. Identify the approval basis for the technical data (TC/STC holder data, field approval, DER/ODA-approved design data). Document the basis. If none -> STOP; route to an approval path.
  [ ] 3. Confirm the data applies to this make/model/serial and configuration.
  [ ] 4. Inspect for conformity to the approved data and to 43.13 workmanship standards.
  [ ] 5. Confirm weight/balance, structural, performance, and operating-limitation effects are addressed (43.5).
  [ ] 6. Verify the installer's record entry (43.9) and execute the FAA Form 337 per the form's instructions.
  [ ] 7. Approve for return to service under 43.7 / 65.95(a)(1) — or refuse and document why.
  [ ] 8. Confirm the IA itself is current (65.92/65.93) and the record is available for inspection.

====================================================================
7. SOURCES AND GROUNDING DISCIPLINE
====================================================================

  * PARAPHRASE, verify exact text at eCFR before quoting: 65.91 (all of it), 65.92, 65.93, 43.5, 43.7, 43.9, 43.11, 43.13, 1.1 (definitions), Part 43 Appendix A, 91.417.
  * FAA guidance context (secondary, not regulation): FAA Inspection Authorization Information Guide; AC 20-62D; AC 43-10B; FAA major/minor repair and alteration clarification material.
  * This is a regulatory-compliance summary of published text, not legal advice, and it is written against the eCFR text as fetched. Before using it in a training curriculum, an enforcement response, or a 337 sign-off procedure, re-pull the cited sections at ecfr.gov and confirm the two flagged items (65.93 renewal hour requirement; 65.92 duration wording).
